title: Resilience Fund beneficiaries hold no acquired right, so recognition confers expectation rather than entitlement
content:
A.2.9.1.1.1.3.3.1 is blunt: "[p]ersons qualified as beneficiaries do not have any acquired right or claim." Payout is "subject to the approval of the Resilience Technical Committee (at their sole and absolute discretion) and further contingent on a SKY vote endorsing payment of the claim." The application terms (A.2.9.1.1.1.4.1.4) make the applicant affirm the same thing — participation is opt-in, the terms "can be amended at any time," and registration "does not give rise to any right, benefit, entitlement, or claim, nor creates an obligation on any party to pay."

The legal reason is clear enough: an enforceable promise to indemnify would make the fund an insurance product and Sky an insurer, with the licensing and liability that follow. Discretion keeps it a gift.

The functional problem is that the fund's purpose is to give contributors the confidence to take actions that attract legal risk, and confidence is exactly what a fully discretionary, revocable, vote-contingent promise fails to supply. A beneficiary sued for governance work must retain counsel *before* knowing whether SKY holders will endorse reimbursement.

The two-key structure compounds this. The Technical Committee's discretion is absolute, and even its approval only unlocks a Governance Poll — so the person most likely to need the fund is asking an electorate to fund a defense whose details are sensitive and encrypted, at the moment their conduct is under external attack.
description: Payout needs Resilience Technical Committee approval at sole and absolute discretion AND a SKY vote endorsing it; applicants sign that registration creates no right, benefit, or obligation to pay.
